require()
 Mechanism

-- Load module (Lua searches package.path for module file)

-- Second require returns cached module (doesn't re-execute)

utils == utils2         -- true (same instance)

-- To force reload, clear cache
package.loaded["utils"] = nil
local utils3 = require("utils")  -- re-executed

utils == utils2         -- true (same instance)

Submodules
Modules can require other modules:

  api_url = "https://prod-api.example.com",
  timeout = 10000,
  -- inherit from default
  retries = default.timeout // 5000
}

encapsulation-with-local-variables
Encapsulation with Local Variables
Use local variables for private state:
-- cache.lua
local cache_data = {}  -- private to this module

local M = {}

function M.get(key)
  return cache_data[key]
end

function M.set(key, value)
  cache_data[key] = value
end

function M.clear()
  cache_data = {}
end

return M
-- cache.lua
local cache_data = {}  -- private to this module
function M.get(key)
  return cache_data[key]
function M.set(key, value)
  cache_data[key] = value
function M.clear()
  cache_data = {}
Users can't access 
cache_data
 directly:
local cache = require("cache")

cache.set("foo", "bar")
print(cache.get("foo"))         -- "bar"
print(cache.cache_data)         -- nil (private)
local cache = require("cache")
cache.set("foo", "bar")
print(cache.get("foo"))         -- "bar"
print(cache.cache_data)         -- nil (private)

pattern-3-class-like-module
Pattern 3: Class-Like Module
-- Point.lua
local Point = {}
Point.__index = Point

function Point.new(x, y)
  local self = setmetatable({x = x, y = y}, Point)
  return self
end

function Point:distance()
  return math.sqrt(self.x ^ 2 + self.y ^ 2)
end

function Point:__tostring()
  return "(" .. self.x .. ", " .. self.y .. ")"
end

return Point

circular-dependencies
Circular Dependencies
If module A requires B and B requires A, you can hit circular dependency issues:
-- a.lua
local B = require("b")
local M = {}
function M.funcA()
  return B.funcB()
end
return M

-- b.lua
local A = require("a")  -- circular!
local M = {}
function M.funcB()
  return A.funcA()  -- may be incomplete
end
return M
-- a.lua
local B = require("b")
function M.funcA()
  return B.funcB()
-- b.lua
local A = require("a")  -- circular!
function M.funcB()
  return A.funcA()  -- may be incomplete
Solution: delay the require or use a different pattern:
-- a.lua
local M = {}
function M.funcA()
  local B = require("b")  -- require inside function
  return B.funcB()
end
return M

-- b.lua
local M = {}
function M.funcB()
  local A = require("a")
  return A.funcA()
end
return M
  local B = require("b")  -- require inside function
  local A = require("a")
  return A.funcA()
global-vs-module-variables
Global vs Module Variables
Best practice: keep modules self-contained:
-- bad.lua (pollutes globals)
CONFIG = {timeout = 5000}

function helper()
  return CONFIG.timeout
end

return {helper = helper}

-- good.lua (contained)
local CONFIG = {timeout = 5000}

local function helper()
  return CONFIG.timeout
end

return {helper = helper}
-- bad.lua (pollutes globals)
CONFIG = {timeout = 5000}
function helper()
  return CONFIG.timeout
return {helper = helper}
-- good.lua (contained)

local function helper()

️-edge-cases-gotchas
⚠️ Edge Cases & Gotchas
Module name must match filename
require("math_utils")
 loads 
math_utils.lua
 (or in subdirectory with 
 separator).
 caches globally
: All uses of 
require("foo")
 get the same instance. Modifications affect all users.
Search path is searched in order
: First match wins. If you have name conflicts, the one in earlier paths takes precedence.
No namespace privacy
: Module tables are just tables. Users can modify returned table: 
utils.add = function() return 0 end
 (bad practice, but possible).
Circular requires can fail unpredictably
: If modules access each other at load time (not function time), you can get nil errors.
Large files loaded completely
 loads and executes the entire file. For huge modules, consider lazy loading inside functions.

🧠 Spot the Bug
What happens here?
-- a.lua
print("Loading A")
local B = require("b")
print("Loaded A")
return {name = "A"}

-- b.lua
print("Loading B")
local A = require("a")
print("Loaded B")
return {name = "B"}

-- main.lua
require("a")
print("Loading A")
print("Loaded A")
return {name = "A"}
print("Loading B")
local A = require("a")
print("Loaded B")
return {name = "B"}
require("a")
details
summary
Answer
Prints:
text
language-text
Loading A
Loading B
Loaded A
Loaded B
Here's why:
ul
li
Require A: prints "Loading A", then requires B
Require B: prints "Loading B", requires A (already partially loaded, returns the incomplete module)
B finishes: prints "Loaded B"
A finishes: prints "Loaded A"
Both modules complete, but B gets an incomplete version of A (without the return value applied yet). If B tries to access 
A.something
 at load time, it fails.
The lesson
: Avoid circular dependencies at module load time. Use lazy loading (require inside functions) if you need circular dependencies.
